questions.q: What three concrete questions does this lesson break "governance" into?
options: What data exists and where (cataloging), where did a value come from (lineage), and who's responsible for it (ownership)
How much does it cost, how fast does it run, and how much storage does it use
Who wrote the code, when was it written, and what language was used
What SLA applies, what SLO is set, and what the error budget is
questions.explain: None of these has an obvious answer once a platform has dozens of tables, several pipelines, and multiple teams.

questions.q: What does Microsoft Purview provide for Fabric, and what is its Databricks parallel?
options: A searchable catalog of workspace items, serving the same purpose as Databricks & Delta Lake's Unity Catalog (Lesson 38)
A billing dashboard with no relationship to any Databricks concept
A real-time alerting mechanism, parallel to Activator
A backup and disaster recovery tool with no Databricks equivalent
questions.explain: Different implementation, identical underlying purpose — making data findable across a growing platform.

questions.q: What does data lineage help answer, according to this lesson?
options: Which of several transformation stages introduced an error, by tracing a value back through everything that produced it
How much a specific pipeline costs to run each month
Who has permission to edit a specific KQL Queryset
How long a pipeline has been running without failure
questions.explain: This mirrors Databricks & Delta Lake's Lesson 44 concept, applied here to a real-time pipeline instead of a batch one.

questions.q: How does this lesson's concept of ownership relate to Lesson 44's data contract?
options: The data contract established a producer/consumer relationship for one dataset; ownership generalizes that to every table, Eventstream, and dashboard needing a named, accountable owner
Ownership and data contracts are unrelated concepts with no connection
Ownership replaces the need for a data contract entirely
Only Eventstreams need an owner, not tables or dashboards
questions.explain: The owner isn't necessarily the only person who can touch it, but the accountable first point of contact.

questions.q: Why does real-time data raise the governance stakes compared to batch data?
options: A real-time dashboard that's wrong is wrong right now, in front of whoever's watching, unlike a batch report that can be caught and fixed before most people notice
Real-time systems never actually need governance since they update so frequently
Batch systems always have higher governance stakes than real-time ones
There's no real difference in governance stakes between the two
questions.explain: This is exactly why cataloging, lineage, and ownership matter more for real-time systems, not less.
